title: Chapter 38 – Lin Hu
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Hu]

Lin Hu has learned to count the days since his father died in a particular way, by the number of times he has stopped himself from saying my father.

Five hundred and twenty-one, this morning. He keeps the tally in his head, the way Radish does with everything, because it is the only habit of Radish's that he has ever been able to steal. Five hundred and twenty-one times he has opened his mouth to say my father says, or my father would, and shut it again. The word is still there, a stone in his throat. He has simply learned to swallow around it.

He is twelve. He has been twelve for six weeks. He is taller than he was in the spring, thinner, with his father's long jaw and his mother's narrow dark eyes, and he is a Qi Refining fourth-stage with a fire root and a wood root, which in the Lin household is a very ordinary thing to be. He sleeps in a small room off the kitchen, in the east wing, with his mother in the next room, and every night he hears her turn over and not sleep.

He does not know what he is supposed to feel. Nobody has told him.

The burial was held a week after the midsummer, in the heat, and almost nobody came. Not because they hated him. Because nobody knew what to say. A traitor who sells his clan to its enemy, who gets his own son's cousin killed, who betrays his father's dream for the price of a gambling debt, is not a man for whom people weep. They come and stand with their faces blank, and look at the grave, and look away. Aunt Wenqing came. She stood at the edge of the pit with her hands folded and did not look at the coffin, and then she looked at Lin Hu, and she said: I am sorry for your trouble. That was all. It was the kindest thing anyone said.

His father is buried in the lowest corner of the graveyard, under a crooked pine. There is no stone. Old Hu offered to carve one. Lin Hu said no.

* * *

It is the first week of winter, and the market at Willow Ford is loud with the smell of roasting chestnuts.

He has come with Old Fang, who is sixty-five and bent and fond of him in a rough, wordless way, and who has asked him to carry the tally sticks. It is something to do. Aunt Wenjun said it would be good for him to see the town. Mother said nothing. He has walked a mile behind Fang's mule with a bundle of bamboo on his back, and the cold has got into his hands, and he has said nothing for six hours.

At the third stall a boy says, "That is the traitor's son."

Lin Hu does not stop walking. The boy is behind him, near the chestnut vendor, speaking in a carrying voice that has been pitched exactly to reach. He is fourteen, perhaps, with a fat soft face and a green sash at his waist, the sash of a Red Ridge servant's son.

"The one whose father sold the Lins to the Zhao," the boy goes on. "Then the Lins killed him for it, they say. Buried him in the garden. Do you think they have a stone?"

Somebody laughs.

"It was not like that," Lin Hu says. He has turned without deciding to. His voice comes out thin. "My father was killed by the Zhao."

"Is that what they tell you?" The boy shrugs. "It is what everybody in Willow Ford says. That the old Patriarch's boys put a sword in your father's back and left him in a ditch. Who else would? He was a Lin. They are always killing each other. It is why the hill is dying."

The voice is very reasonable. It is the voice of someone who has been told what to say and has said it so many times that he almost believes it.

Lin Hu feels a heat start in his chest.

It is a fire-root heat, a familiar one. He has felt it all his life, the little hot spark under the ribs that his father used to say was the sign of a good cultivator. Never let it out of the door, his father said. Keep it in the house. He has kept it in the house for twelve years.

The Solar Wheel leaves his hand before he knows he has raised it.

It is a small one. A disc of orange light the size of a dinner plate, spinning, whining, and it goes across the six paces between them in the space of a heartbeat and takes the boy's sash, and the cloth under it, and half the skin of his belly. The boy screams. The chestnut vendor drops his tongs. A woman at the next stall cries out and the crowd opens in a ring, and Lin Hu stands in the middle of it with his hand still outstretched and the stink of burnt wool in his nose.

I did not mean—

Yes you did.

He sees the boy on the ground, clutching his stomach. He sees the faces, wide-eyed, and the constable in his brown tunic shouldering through, and Old Fang hobbling up from the mule with his mouth open.

He sees, at the edge of the circle, a young man in a green robe with a splinted right arm, leaning on a pillar with his left hand on the hilt of a saber, watching.

Zhao Qian does not smile. He does not do anything at all. He only lifts his chin, a very small movement, and then turns away and walks off into the crowd.

* * *

Old Fang takes the blame.

It is the first thing that makes Lin Hu feel really ill. The old man puts himself between the constable and the boy, with his bamboo sticks under one arm, and says in his cracked voice that the child was provoked, that a Zhao servant's son has no business saying such things in the street, and that if the constable wants to put someone in the cage he may put old Fang, who has stood at this stall for thirty-one years and has never once had a complaint. He is the kind of man the town trusts. The constable looks at him for a long time and says, very slowly, that it will be a fine of three stones, to be paid by the house of Lin.

Three stones. Lin Hu does the sum. It is nearly the cost of a week of rice for the household.

They drive home in silence in the gray evening, the mule clopping, the cart creaking. Fang does not speak. After the first mile Lin Hu begins, helplessly, to cry. He does not make a sound. He sits with his hands under his arms and the tears running into his collar, looking at the road.

At the gate of the hill Fang says, without turning, "You have a good arm, boy."

"I did not mean—"

"I know." The old man's voice is gentle. "That is the trouble with a good arm. It never does."

He sets him down in the yard. Then he drives away to the stable, without another word.

Lin Hu stands in the dusk with his fists clenched. He expects a crowd. A shout. His mother in tears, or worse, no one at all. There is nobody in the yard but a single tall figure by the well, in a gray cloak, with a gardener's hat in her hand.

Su Qinghe waits until he has come close. She does not say anything. She lifts one hand and, with two fingers, taps him lightly on the forehead.

It is not a blow. It does not hurt. But a cold, clean stillness spreads out from the point of contact, down through his skull and into his chest, like a drop of ink in a bowl of water, and the heat there is gone. It is not extinguished. It is simply put away, folded and laid in a drawer.

"Walk with me," she says.

* * *

They go to the old threshing floor behind the storehouse.

It is a bare yard, flat and hard, with a low wall around three sides and a broken millstone in the middle. The stars are coming out. He has been here before, in the summer, to practice spear forms with Feng, who is gone now. He has never been here in winter. The cold bites through his tunic.

She does not sit. She stands with her back to the wall and her hat in her hands, and looks at him in the last light with those very quiet, very level eyes.

"You are angry," she says.

"I am not."

"You are the angriest boy I have ever seen. I have been looking at you for a year." She says it without heat. "You have kept it in so long that it has gone sour. It comes out at the first chance. It came out today."

"He said—"

"I know what he said." She turns her hat over in her hands. "He was told to say it. A boy in the Zhao household, with a fat face and a green sash. He did not make it up. And Zhao Qian stood at a pillar and watched, because Zhao Qian wanted to see what you would do."

Lin Hu stares at her. "How do you—"

"I have a friend in the market." A very small smile. "It does not matter. What matters is that you gave him what he wanted. A Lin boy, in a rage, in the street. A burn on a Zhao servant's belly. The Registry will hear of it by morning. It will be one more line in the book." She pauses. "Do you understand?"

"I am sorry."

"Do not be sorry. Be quiet." Her voice sharpens. "That is what I am going to teach you. Not to be less angry. I do not think that can be done, and I would not want to do it. To be quiet. There is a difference."

She sets her hat on the millstone. She lifts her left hand and lays the palm flat in the air between them, and he feels, faintly, a cold, steady pressure, like the edge of a pond in winter.

"I am going to show you something," she says. "A very old art. Water makes it. It is called the Still Water Veil, and I have taught it to exactly one other person, who learned it in eleven days. You may be slower. That is no shame. I want you to do exactly what I say, and I want you to feel nothing but what I tell you to feel."

* * *

It takes him nine days.

It is the hardest thing he has ever done, and it is the first thing that has made him feel better in a year.

She is a very strange teacher. She does not shout. She does not demonstrate. She sits cross-legged on the cold stone with her eyes half closed, and she tells him a small thing, and waits. Breathe in until your lungs are full. Hold. Now let it go, and do not let it leave you. He does. It takes him three hours to understand what she means. When he finally does, it is like discovering a muscle he did not know he had.

The Veil, as she explains it, is not a wall. It is not a hiding place. It is a way of holding still inside your own skin. Your Qi is a pond. Most people's ponds are full of ripples, wavelets, little eddies, flashes of heat and light that anyone with a trained sense can feel from forty paces. A fire-root's is the worst. It spits and sparks all the time.

To veil, you do not stop the fire. You fold it under.

"A cloth," Mother says, on the fourth day. "You lay a cloth over a bowl of coals. The coals still burn. But the cloth keeps in the light, and the heat, and the smell. Nobody looks at the bowl. They look at the cloth." She lifts her hand. "You are the cloth. Not the coals. Do you see?"

"I think so."

"Do it again."

He does it again. He does it thirty times a day, in the cold, with his eyes closed, until he can feel the ripple at the center of his chest go flat and still, a mirror of black water, with the heat folded away below it like a stone at the bottom of a well. On the seventh day he notices something odd. When he is veiled, the world is quieter. The anger is still there, but it is far off, a drumbeat in the next valley. He can hear himself think.

On the ninth day Su Qinghe stands in front of him and places her palm over his heart.

"Close your eyes," she says. "Tell me what you feel."

He does. Her hand is warm. Behind it, very faintly, he feels the slow steady rhythm of her Qi, a cool green pulse. And under it, deeper, quieter, a second shape, like a smooth stone at the bottom of a river.

"You are a Qi Refining third-stage," he says. He is not sure how he knows.

"I am." Her voice is calm. "And now?"

She does something. He cannot say what. The pulse under his palm falls silent, and a flat, smooth, empty nothing takes its place, a pond without a ripple, a sky without a cloud.

"Now you are a woman who does not cultivate," he says slowly. "You are a farmer. You are no one."

"Yes." She lowers her hand. "That is what a veil does. It is not magic. It is the art of being a little less than you are, deliberately, until it is useful to be more." She tilts her head. "You are the second person I have taught it to, Lin Hu. I want you to understand what that means. It is a trust. If you tell anyone how to do it, or use it for something that will hurt this house, I will know. And I will not be gentle."

"I will not tell anyone."

"I know." A long pause. "I wish you had come to it earlier, and by a different road. But you came. That is the part that matters."

She picks up her hat and puts it on. He realizes, with a small odd shock, that he does not hate her. He has hated her for a year, since the morning she took him by the arm and said, In this house, that means you eat. He has hated her for being kind to him when he did not want to be.

He does not hate her now.

"Thank you, Aunt," he says.

She stops with her hand on the wall. She does not turn around.

"Do not thank me," she says. "Go and thank the one who made it possible."

"Who?"

But she is already gone, a gray shape in the dusk, her footsteps making no sound on the frozen ground.

* * *

He thinks about it for a week.

The second person. He turns it over and over. The first one learned in eleven days. There are very few people it could be. Not Feng, who leaves a trail of burnt grass wherever he goes. Not Yue, who is six. Not Father, who is dead.

He knows. He has known for days. He simply has not said it.

He begins to watch.

He watches the way other people do not, at the edges, with the Veil folded over his own Qi so that nobody notices him looking. It is surprisingly easy. A boy of twelve who is quiet and sullen and does not speak is the most invisible creature in the world. He sits at the back of the kitchen with a bowl of rice and watches Jian eat.

Radish eats fast. He eats like a person who has places to be. His hands are small and square, with a long red scar along the right forearm, and the nails are bitten short. When he thinks nobody is watching, his eyes go still, as though he were looking at a page nobody else can see.

He counts, Lin Hu thinks. He counts the rice.

He watches him in the yard. A day later, in the passage by the library. Two days later, in the granary, where the old refiner is bellowing at Kai about the crucible and Jian stands at the bench with a ruler and a slip of paper and says things in a low voice that make the old man stop shouting. Lin Hu stands in the doorway for an hour, with his arms folded, and does not understand a word of what he hears. But he understands the look on Hu's face, which is not the look of a man teaching a pupil. It is the look of a man listening to a colleague.

He is the only person in the house who is not afraid of the old man.

And one evening, on the fourteenth day, he sees something that does not make sense.

He is crossing the yard to the well with an empty bucket, in the blue dusk, and Jian is ahead of him, walking fast with his head down. Something moves under the front of his tunic. A small, round, scaled shape bulges and shifts, and for an instant a tiny pale snout pokes out of the collar and sniffs the air.

Lin Hu stops dead.

Jian does too. He does not turn. He stands for a long moment with his back to him in the dusk. Then, very slowly, he looks over his shoulder.

"It is a lizard," he says.

"It has scales."

"Lizards do."

"It has a face like a pebble." It comes out more sharply than he means it to. "It is the size of a loaf of bread."

"It is a very large lizard."

They look at each other. Jian's face in the dusk is perfectly composed, a ten-year-old's face, smooth and patient and plain. But under the plainness there is something else, an alertness, a cold, steady readiness, like a cat that has seen a hawk's shadow cross the grass.

He is deciding whether to lie to me again, Lin Hu thinks. And whether I am someone he has to lie to.

He says nothing.

For a long time, neither of them moves. Then, at last, he lifts the bucket in his hand and holds it up, a small pointless gesture.

"I am going to get water," he says. "I have not seen anything."

A breath. The faintest shift in the cold small face.

"The lizard likes salt," Jian says. "If you have any."

"I will bring some."

"Thank you."

He goes to the well. He draws the water. He carries it back across the yard with his arms aching in the cold, and does not look at the shape in the tunic, which has gone very still.

It is not a lizard, he thinks, and for no reason that he can name, he feels a warmth in his chest that has nothing to do with fire.

* * *

On the last night of the month he goes to the graveyard.

It is a still, bitter night, with frost on the stones and a thin moon over the pines. The wall of the burying ground is low, and the gate is open. He walks through the dark between the old tablets, past the long gray stone that says Lin Zhenshan. Patriarch. He held the hill, past the founder's mound, to the lowest corner under the crooked pine.

There is no stone. There is a low mound, and a hollow where the earth has sunk, and a handful of withered grass.

He stands over it for a long time with his hands in his sleeves.

He had not meant to say anything. He has not been able to think of what to say. But he finds, standing there, that his mouth has begun to move on its own.

"I have been learning the Veil," he says.

The wind stirs the pine. A little powdery frost slides down.

"You did a terrible thing. I know it. The whole house knows. I have heard it in a hundred ways, from a hundred people who were careful not to say it to my face. It is true. You were a coward, and you were weak, and you gave a boy to a wolf." His voice does not break. It is very quiet. "Bo would have been eighteen. He used to save the last rice ball for Yue. I did not know that, until the day he died."

He swallows.

"I am not going to say I forgive you. I do not. Maybe I will, someday. Maybe not." A pause. "But I want you to know that I am going to do something with this. The Veil. And whatever comes after. I do not know what yet. I only know it is not going to be what you did."

The frost glitters. The pine creaks.

He puts his hand in the pocket of his tunic, and takes out a small flat object wrapped in a scrap of cloth. It is a pencil case, silver, with a worn brass cap. It has been in his possession for a year. He found it in his father's room, under the bed, after the funeral, and he has carried it in his pocket ever since, a cold, heavy thing, without once looking at it.

He knows what it is. He has known since the day the library roof was ruined. There are two parallel scratches on the brass cap, four millimeters apart, and a little curl of gray tile-dust still caught in the hinge.

He crouches. He digs in the frozen earth beside the mound with his bare fingers, until his nails split, and lays the pencil case in the hole and covers it.

"There," he says. "That is where it belongs."

He gets to his feet. The moon is almost down. He has been here too long, and the cold has gone through him to the bone. He turns for the gate.

And stops.

On the wall of the graveyard, forty paces away, a figure sits. Small, and very still, hunched on the stone with its knees drawn up and a faint pale shape curled in its lap. It is looking at him.

It does not speak. It does not move. It simply watches, in the starlight, with the grave composure of a child who has been waiting for hours and has decided not to be noticed.

Lin Hu stands in the frost and meets his eyes.

He followed me, he thinks. He has been here the whole time. He heard.

He waits for the contempt. For the question. For the you were crying, you were praying to a traitor. None of it comes. The small figure on the wall only lifts one hand, very slowly, and makes the sign that the clan makes at a funeral. A fist pressed to the chest. Then it lowers it again and sits there, in the cold, keeping vigil.

It is the kindest thing anyone has done for him in a year.

I have not got a Veil good enough for this, Lin Hu thinks, and wipes his face with his sleeve. Not yet.

He crosses the frozen ground to the wall. He climbs up beside his cousin, who makes room for him without a word, and the two of them sit together in the dark with the little scaled creature warm between them, watching the moon go down behind the pines, and nobody says anything at all.

After a while, Jian says softly, "I count the days too."

"Five hundred and thirty-five."

"Five hundred and thirty-five." A pause. "I will carry baskets in the morning, if you want company."

"I will carry them," Lin Hu says. "You count them."

It is not quite a laugh that comes out of Jian. It is a short, breathy sound, as of a small thing finding itself unexpectedly warm. He does not say anything else. He does not need to.

Beyond the wall, on the black slope of Red Ridge, a single light is burning in the dark.

It has been burning every night for a month. Lin Hu looks at it for a long time. For the first time in his life, he does not think of it as a place where his father went. He thinks of it as a place he is going to have to deal with.

One day, he thinks, and folds the thought away, quiet as a coal under a cloth. Not tonight.
